query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid machine learning model that incorporates defect-aware electronic transport theory and high-throughput conductivity data will predict the conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr (with ~1 wt.% oxygen) across both cryogenic (0–200 K) and high-temperature (300–1200 K) regimes with significantly improved accuracy relative to conventional analytical models that assume perfect, defect‐free crystals.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen, produced by additive manufacturing methods that inherently introduce grain-boundary defects and oxygen interstitials.
generation.intervention: Apply a hybrid machine learning framework that couples defect-aware electronic transport theory with systematic high-throughput conductivity measurements across 0–1200 K, including key microstructural parameters such as defect density and grain size.
generation.conditions: Measurements conducted in two temperature regimes: 0–200 K (cryogenic) and 300–1200 K (high temperature), using specimens with ~1 wt.% oxygen and similar processing histories to ensure consistent defect profiles.
generation.structural_mediator: Oxygen-induced defects and microstructural irregularities (e.g., dislocation density and grain boundary characteristics) that mediate electron/phonon scattering and alter conduction properties.
generation.mechanism: By integrating experimental conductivity data and accounting for defect/oxygen effects, the ML framework captures additional scattering mechanisms not present in idealized models. This refined parameterization reduces predictive error by explicitly modeling the impact of real-world imperfections on conduction behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will yield conductivity predictions within a 10% margin of the experimentally measured values, particularly at a withheld benchmark temperature (e.g., 250 K), outperforming conventional analytical approaches that do not incorporate defect effects.
generation.baseline: Traditional analytical models that assume perfect, defect‐free crystalline structures, which typically show larger discrepancies when compared to experimental measurements on oxygen-doped specimens.
generation.boundary: Applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with ~1 wt.% oxygen processed through additive manufacturing. The model’s predictions are validated only within the temperature range of 0–200 K and 300–1200 K; predictions outside these ranges or for significantly different oxygen contents may not be reliable.
generation.uncertainty: The precise extent of error reduction is uncertain and may vary with uncharacterized defect states, extreme temperature effects, or variations in oxygen distribution. Further experimental validation across diverse samples is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Train the hybrid ML model on a comprehensive dataset incorporating conductivity measurements across 0–1200 K for HfNbTaTiZr with ~1 wt.% oxygen, withholding the measurement at 250 K. Fabricate new specimens under the same processing conditions, measure their conductivity at 250 K, and compare these values to the model’s predictions.
measurements: Conductivity (electrical or thermal) of specimens at 250 K
Quantification of oxygen content and characterization of defect density via microstructural analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the model’s predicted conductivity at 250 K deviates by more than 10% from the experimentally measured value, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In this study, the wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy coating was systematically analyzed by the molecular dynamics method. FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy was used as a coating material to adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix. The friction and nanoindentation simulation of this coating material were carried out by controlling the ambient temperature. The influence of temperature on its friction properties was analyzed on five aspects: lattice structure, dislocation evolution, friction coefficient, hardness, and elastic modulus. The results show that with the increase of temperature, the disorder of the lattice structure increases, which leads to an increase of the tangential force and friction coefficient in the friction process. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . Abstract The microstructure, temperature-dependent mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) additively manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) were investigated. SLM-built HEA had a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase random solid solution. In addition, SLM-built HEA was composed of epitaxial growth grains, dislocation network and nano-sized oxides. Room- and high-temperature compression tests confirmed that SLM-built HEA has outstanding mechanical properties in all temperature ranges compared to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEAs reported up to the present. The excellent mechanical properties of SLM-built HEA were achieved with fine grains, high dislocation density and fine precipitates at low temperatures (25 °C to 600 °C), and by high dislocation density and fine precipitates at high temperatures (700 °C or higher). On the other hand, the deformation microstructure showed that slip and deformation twins are the main deformation mechanisms from 25 °C to 600 °C, and slip and partial recrystallization are the main deformation mechanisms above 700 °C. The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available. Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] . High strength and ductility, often mutually exclusive properties of a structural material, are also responsible for damage tolerance. At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity. In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility. In this study, we have examined the temperature-dependent superplasticity of single component Ag and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires using molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior. Interestingly, HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures. decision.trend: In 2019, researchers examined equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr processed by various powder metallurgy routes and revealed how oxygen content (0.12–0.2 wt.%) influenced the alloy’s microstructure and mechanical performance (PMC6926650). In 2020, they explored doping HfNbTaTiZr-like compositions with ~2 at.% oxygen to improve damping and high-temperature strength, though conductivity modeling was not addressed (PMC7299626). By 2024, additive manufacturing was used to fabricate bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing ~1 wt.% oxygen, testing mechanical and oxidation behavior up to ~1100 °C (PMC11077685). These studies confirmed oxygen’s strong impact on material properties but did not rigorously predict conductivity across wide temperature ranges, leaving the conduction response largely unexplored and unmodeled under real defect conditions.
decision.unsolved: There is still no robust, experimentally validated predictive model that captures how ~1 wt.% oxygen and other lattice imperfections affect the thermal or electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr from near 0–200 K to 300–1200 K. Conventional analytical formulations often assume perfect crystals and thus produce large errors when dealing with real alloys that contain interstitials and other defects.
decision.lever: Develop a hybrid ML-augmented framework coupling defect-aware electronic transport theory with systematic high-throughput data on compositions, temperatures (0–1200 K), and measured oxygen contents (~1 wt.%) to refine predictions of conduction properties. Key model parameters: doping levels, temperature dependence, microstructural (grain size, defect density) data.
decision.why: A data-driven model incorporating oxygen-driven scattering effects and temperature-dependent transport has the potential to surpass purely analytical, defect-free assumptions. Prior studies show that oxygen alters mechanical and transport behavior, yet the conduction response across broad temperatures remains insufficiently captured. By training on partial doping and temperature-dependent data—and by incorporating known electron scattering physics—this approach can systematically reduce predictive errors. The hypothesis will be tested by comparing predicted conductivity at a withheld temperature (e.g., 250 K) for a 1 wt.% oxygen sample against newly measured data. A deviation bigger than 10% from the measured benchmark would falsify the hypothesis.
